claims.text: Equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni contains intrinsic nanoscale short-range chemical ordering.
The initial material has minimal preexisting defect clustering.
Minor alloying additions can fine-tune point-defect mobilities.
Nanoscale chemical ordering balances vacancy and interstitial mobilities.
Chemical ordering provides energetically favorable sites for vacancy–interstitial recombination.
Enhanced vacancy–interstitial recombination limits irradiation-induced defect accumulation and damage.
The interaction between nanoscale chemical ordering and radiation-induced defect clusters mediates efficient recombination.
Reduced irradiation-induced defect accumulation stabilizes the alloy phase.
The proposed self-healing mechanism preserves high-temperature strength, environmental or oxidation resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
Low-energy 40 keV He2+ irradiation can be used to produce and study near-surface radiation damage.
The controlled experiment will compare irradiation at room and cryogenic temperatures.
Samples retaining chemical order will exhibit minimal irradiation-induced swelling.
Samples retaining chemical order will exhibit less irradiation hardening than the baseline.
Irradiation may retain or slightly improve nanoscale chemical ordering.
Rapid quenching or compositional tuning can deliberately disrupt intrinsic chemical ordering.
Under identical irradiation, chemically ordered samples will accumulate fewer radiation-induced defects than order-disrupted samples.
Equivalent or better irradiation resistance in the order-disrupted samples would falsify the proposed ordering-mediated mechanism.
The hypothesis is restricted primarily to equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni under conditions representative of 40 keV He2+ exposure.

contradictions.description: The prediction describes reduced irradiation-induced swelling and hardening relative to a baseline that may be non-irradiated. A non-irradiated sample does not experience irradiation-induced swelling or hardening, so this comparison cannot establish a reduction relative to that control.

The baseline conflates two distinct controls—non-irradiated material and order-disrupted material—whereas the falsification experiment appropriately compares ordered and disrupted samples under identical irradiation. Treating these controls as interchangeable confounds irradiation effects with ordering effects.
